title: Mu'tah
hook: He named three commanders in order, in case each fell. Then he told the news with tears before any messenger arrived.
glossary: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un

screens.text: **He named three commanders, in order, in case each one fell.** Then, in Madinah, he told the people what had happened, with tears in his eyes, before any messenger arrived.

**An army heads north.** In 8 AH the Prophet ﷺ sent an army toward Byzantine lands. He didn't go himself. At a place called Mu'tah it met a much larger force, IslamQA reports [IslamQA 11575; IslamQA 305386].
bubbles: We tell the history, not the battle. His rule of war stood: no harming women or children [Bukhari 3015].

screens.prompt: He named the commanders in order: if one fell, the next would lead. Put them in his order [Bukhari 4261].
screens.feedback: Zayd first. If Zayd fell, Ja'far. If Ja'far fell, 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah [Bukhari 4261].

screens.text: **Two men he loved.** The first two names weren't strangers. Zayd had grown up in his house. Ja'far was his cousin, home from Abyssinia only about a year. Sending them north meant risking the people closest to him.

cards.back: Kidnapped as a child and sold, then freed by the Prophet ﷺ and raised as his son, the early biographers say. Among the very first believers [Qalam ep. 32; IslamQA 11575].
His cousin, who spoke for the Muslims before the king of Abyssinia and recited from Surah Maryam, the early reports say [Qalam ep. 43; Dar al-Ifta 175].
Named third: if Ja'far fell, he was to lead [Bukhari 4261].

events.title: Khaybar
events.text: Ja'far comes home from Abyssinia, the early biographers report [Dar al-Ifta 175].

events.title: An army goes north
events.text: Toward Byzantine lands, under three named commanders [Bukhari 4261].

events.title: Three commanders fall
events.text: Zayd, then Ja'far, then Ibn Rawahah [Bukhari 4262].

events.title: Tears before the news
events.text: He tells the people himself, weeping, before any messenger arrives [Bukhari 4262].

events.title: Next: Makkah
events.text: He returns to the city that drove him out.

screens.text: **News before the messenger.** In Madinah, before any messenger came, he told the people: Zayd took the flag and was killed, then Ja'far, then Ibn Rawahah. As he spoke, his eyes were streaming with tears [Bukhari 4262].
bubbles: Then he said that one of Allah's swords, Khalid, had taken the flag, and Allah had given them victory [Bukhari 4262].

screens.prompt: He wept openly as he gave the news. Why does that matter?

options.text: It shows that grief isn't a lack of faith
options.feedback: Right. The most patient of people still wept for those he loved.

options.text: It shows he doubted Allah's plan
options.feedback: Not quite. Tears aren't doubt. He called them mercy when his son died [Bukhari 1303].

options.text: It shows leaders should hide their feelings
options.feedback: Not quite. He did the opposite: he let people see him grieve.

screens.text: **Tears aren't weakness.** In Day 64 you saw him weep as his baby son died, calling it mercy [Bukhari 1303]. At Mu'tah he wept for a son he had raised and a cousin he loved. If you're grieving someone, you're in his company.

screens.situation: Jordan's best friend from high school died in a car crash last week. At the masjid, a man tells Jordan that Muslims accept Allah's decree, so there's no need to cry.

options.text: Let himself grieve, cry if he needs to, and pray for comfort
options.feedback: Yes. Accepting Allah's decree and crying go together. The Prophet ﷺ did both.

options.text: Hold it all in to prove his faith is strong
options.feedback: Not quite. Bottled grief doesn't prove anything. He wept openly and called it mercy [Bukhari 1303].

options.text: Decide he must be a weak Muslim for feeling this way
options.feedback: Not quite. Sadness isn't weak faith. Even the Prophet ﷺ cried when he lost people he loved.

chips: Who was Khalid, the "sword of Allah"?
Did the Muslims win at Mu'tah?
I'm grieving. What does Islam say?

screens.text: Let grief be honest, yours or someone else's.
steps: If you're missing someone, say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un ("Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return") [Q 2:156]
Tell one trusted person how you're really doing, or check on a friend who's grieving

screens.text: He chose his commanders with care, and he wept when they fell. Faith and tears can live in the same heart.
Next episode: the city that drove him out opens its gates, and he takes no revenge.

check.prompt: Who did he name first to command the army at Mu'tah?

options.feedback: Right. Then Ja'far, then 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah, each in case the one before fell [Bukhari 4261].
Not quite. Zayd was first. Khalid took the flag only after all three named commanders fell [Bukhari 4262].

check.prompt: How did he give the news of their deaths?

options.text: Himself, with tears in his eyes, before any messenger arrived
options.feedback: Right. He grieved openly for the people he loved [Bukhari 4262].

options.text: Calmly, without any sign of sadness
options.feedback: Not quite. His eyes were streaming with tears as he spoke [Bukhari 4262].

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- In 8 AH he sent an army north toward Byzantine lands; it met a much larger force at Mu'tah [IslamQA 11575 ("the Romans gathered a huge army")]. IslamQA 305386 lists it among his campaigns though he didn't go himself. Single organisation: say "IslamQA reports" or "much larger". Don't give army sizes (3,000 and larger figures are sirah only).
- He appointed Zayd ibn Harithah, then Ja'far if Zayd was killed, then 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah if Ja'far was killed [Bukhari 4261].
- All three were killed. He told the people before the news arrived, with tears in his eyes, then said a sword from Allah's swords (Khalid) took the flag and Allah gave them victory [Bukhari 4262].
- Zayd: one of the first believers; a former slave he had freed and raised as a son [Qalam ep. 32; IslamQA 11575]. (scholar question Q40)
- Ja'far: his cousin; spoke for the Muslims before the Negus and recited from Surah Maryam [Qalam ep. 43; Dar al-Ifta Egypt, seerah part 9]; returned from Abyssinia after Khaybar (7 AH) [Dar al-Ifta Egypt, seerah part 9].
- His rules of war: no killing of women or children [Bukhari 3015]. (scholar question Q39)

**Likely questions**
- *"Did the Muslims win at Mu'tah?"* Historians describe the outcome differently. Use the hadith's words: Khalid took the flag and Allah gave them victory [Bukhari 4262]. Don't add numbers or battle detail.
- *"Who was Zayd? Was he a slave?"* Say plainly: slavery existed everywhere then; Zayd had been kidnapped as a child and sold; the Prophet ﷺ freed him and raised him as a son, and he became one of the first believers. Don't claim slavery is acceptable today; detailed questions go to the imam. (The later change to adoption rules is not taught here; route to the imam.) (scholar question Q40)
- *"Why fight the Byzantines?"* Keep it to history; IslamQA reports a large Roman army gathered. No rulings on fighting today (Day 71 frame). (scholar question Q39)
- *"I'm grieving. What does Islam say?"* Listen first. Tears are mercy [Bukhari 1303]; patience and "we belong to Allah and to Him we return" [Q 2:155–157]; Day 77 covers grief in full. If the person who died wasn't Muslim, follow Day 77's handling: comfort first, no comment on anyone's fate, offer the imam. (scholar question Q23)

**Escalate:** a convert's deceased non-Muslim relative (Q23); detailed questions on slavery or adoption (Q40); fighting today (imam); grief that sounds like depression or crisis (safety rule and mentor).

**Don't**
- Don't describe wounds or the fighting (Bukhari 4261's detail about Ja'far's wounds is not for screens or the AI guide's own initiative).
- Don't call tears weak faith or rush a grieving convert to "be patient".
- Don't comment on any non-Muslim relative's fate.
